strengths: Originality: Using current forward activations to guide ZO perturbations is a sensible and potentially useful extension of random low-rank perturbations. Although the identity G = QHᵀ is standard, exploiting it through online subspace extraction provides a concrete methodological contribution.

Significance: Tables 1–2 show encouraging downstream improvements across two model families. On Qwen3-0.6B, AGZO exceeds both ZO baselines on seven of eight tasks; on Pangu-1B, its reported average improves from MeZO’s 0.706 to 0.720.
The memory results directly support a practical advantage: Figures 3–4 show that activation guidance adds very little peak memory relative to MeZO and LOZO across batch sizes and sequence lengths.

Presentation and technical merits: Algorithms 1–2 clearly explain subspace extraction and in-place updates. The fixed-subspace, single-layer cosine formula in Theorem 5.4 provides a useful characterization of the tradeoff between dimensionality reduction and retained gradient signal.
weaknesses: Soundness: Proposition 5.1 does not correctly account for the dependence of A on the same minibatch B used to estimate the update. Conditioning on A changes the distribution of B, so the conditional expectation cannot generally be identified with the projected gradient of the unconditional population objective F defined in Eq. (14). Appendix A.3 establishes a fixed-batch, fixed-basis identity, but its subsequent averaging does not resolve this dependence. Moreover, differentiating with a frozen basis is different from differentiating an objective whose basis varies with W. The claimed population-objective interpretation needs correction.

The alignment guarantee does not directly describe Algorithm 2. Equation (22) uses a single-layer directional derivative, whereas the implemented algorithm uses one shared scalar containing contributions from every perturbed layer. These other contributions affect the sign and normalization of each layer’s update. The manuscript acknowledges the idealized setting, but extrapolates its result too strongly to the full algorithm. It also does not analyze the approximation error from three power iterations or validate the upstream-gradient condition in Eq. (33).

Reproducibility and statistical reliability are inadequate. Section 6 mentions grid search without providing search ranges, selected learning rates, task-specific batch sizes and sequence lengths, prompts, data quantities, or checkpoint-selection details. Evaluation metrics and the split used for reported scores are insufficiently specified. Appendix B supplies precision and one perturbation parameter but does not close these gaps. No repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates are reported, making modest improvements and results on small benchmarks difficult to assess.

Baseline fidelity is unclear. Equation (2) presents MeZO using f(W + μu) − f(W), whereas standard MeZO uses a symmetric finite difference. The manuscript should establish whether the experiments reproduce the published baselines or use modified one-sided versions, and quantify any effect. This matters because changing the estimator can change finite-radius bias and performance at the same two-query budget.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate activation guidance or establish computational efficiency. There are no rank or power-iteration ablations, no matched random orthonormal-subspace control, and no wall-clock or time-to-quality measurements. All reported AGZO experiments use rank one, while the strongest gradient-retention evidence in Figure 1 concerns rank ten and shows weak rank-one retention in several layers. The claim that forward evaluations dominate runtime remains unverified.

Significance and limitations: Evaluation is restricted to 0.6B–1B models and predominantly language-understanding tasks, so broader LLM fine-tuning claims remain provisional. Comparisons against memory-efficient first-order adaptation would better establish practical usefulness. The discussion should more explicitly acknowledge this scope, the absence of convergence guarantees for the adaptive minibatch subspaces, and the unmeasured runtime overhead. The standard impact statement raises no identifiable material ethical concern; the rejection is driven by technical and evidential gaps.

strengths: Originality: Using current forward activations to guide ZO perturbations is a useful methodological idea. Although the identity ∇Wf = QHᵀ is standard, exploiting it through an online activation subspace provides a concrete contribution beyond random low-rank perturbations.

Soundness within the idealized setting: Theorem 5.4 gives an informative expected-cosine formula for a fixed subspace and an isolated layer. It clearly exposes the tradeoff between reducing perturbation dimension and retaining gradient information.

Significance: Tables 1–2 show promising performance across two model families and several tasks. AGZO beats both ZO baselines on seven of eight Qwen tasks and improves the reported Pangu average from 0.706 for MeZO to 0.720. Figures 3–4 support negligible additional peak memory in the tested configurations.

Presentation: The gradient factorization, subspace extraction, and in-place update are explained through explicit equations and pseudocode. The combination of downstream results, alignment diagnostics, and memory measurements is well motivated.
weaknesses: Soundness—population smoothing claim: Proposition 5.1 conditions on A but averages over minibatches as though their distribution remained unchanged. Algorithm 2 constructs A from the same minibatch used to evaluate the loss, so conditioning on A generally changes the distribution of B. Appendix A.3 establishes a fixed-batch, fixed-basis identity; simply averaging does not establish the stated population identity with F. Furthermore, differentiating an objective whose basis changes with W requires accounting for that dependence. The paper should restrict its interpretation to a frozen-basis, per-batch identity or supply an analysis of the adaptive algorithm.

Soundness—the directional theory does not directly describe the implemented multilayer estimator. Equation (22) uses the layer-specific scalar ⟨Gℓ, Δℓ⟩, whereas Algorithm 2 uses one shared loss difference whose noiseless limit is Σj⟨Gj, Δj⟩. Other layers therefore affect each layer's update direction. Their contributions cancel in the estimator's expectation but do not automatically cancel inside cosine similarity. The isolated-layer result is useful, but the manuscript overstates its implication for the actual training algorithm. Theorem 5.7 also asserts a strict inequality that its assumptions do not guarantee: equal singular values and equal positive Bii give an energy ratio exactly r/s. Its proof silently assumes strictly decreasing singular values.

Empirical reliability and reproducibility are inadequate. Section 6 reports grid search without specifying search ranges or selected settings, and omits essential details such as task-specific batch sizes, learning rates, prompts, evaluation metrics, checkpoint selection, and random seeds. Appendix B supplies precision and one perturbation magnitude but does not close these gaps. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, making small improvements and results on small evaluation sets difficult to assess. It is also unclear whether reported scores use a held-out split distinct from the validation data used for selection.

Baseline fidelity needs clarification. Equations (2) and (4) describe forward differences using f(W + μΔ) − f(W), while standard MeZO uses a symmetric difference. The manuscript does not explain whether its experiments use the original baseline implementations or these modified estimators. This matters because finite-difference bias and numerical behavior can affect the comparison. A faithful baseline comparison and an estimator-choice control are needed.

Mechanistic validation is incomplete. Experiments use rank one, but Section 3 primarily motivates gradient preservation at rank ten or above; Figure 1 shows weak rank-one overlap in several layers. There are no rank or power-iteration ablations, nor a matched random orthonormal-subspace control to isolate activation guidance from perturbation scaling and dimensionality. The upstream-gradient condition in Equation (33) is not empirically checked, and the structural study uses GPT-2 rather than the two models used for downstream evaluation.

Significance and limitations: Practical efficiency is established only for peak memory, not runtime or time to target quality. Every linear layer performs subspace extraction each iteration, yet no timing measurements substantiate the claim that this overhead is lightweight. Evaluation is limited to 0.6B–1B models, and the FO comparison uses 1,000 steps versus 20,000 ZO steps without a compute-matched analysis. The manuscript acknowledges idealized theoretical assumptions but does not adequately discuss these applicability and evaluation limits. The generic impact statement raises no evident material ethical concern; the decisive barriers to acceptance are technical and evidential.

strengths: Originality: Using current forward activations to guide ZO perturbations is a useful extension of random low-rank perturbations. The gradient factorization in Eq. (8) provides a clear motivation, and Algorithms 1–2 describe a simple implementation.

Significance: The reported downstream gains are promising. On Qwen3-0.6B, AGZO exceeds both ZO baselines on seven of eight tasks, including substantial improvements on CB and RTE. Figures 3–4 support the claim of negligible additional peak memory in the tested configurations.

Soundness: The fixed-subspace Gaussian identity and isolated-layer cosine formula in Theorem 5.4 provide useful mathematical understanding of the tradeoff between subspace dimension and captured gradient signal.

Presentation and ethics: The main algorithmic narrative is understandable, and the pseudocode makes the intended mechanism concrete. The use of existing models and benchmarks raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—population smoothing claim: Proposition 5.1 conditions on A while averaging over minibatches as though A were independent of the batch. In Algorithm 2, A is extracted from that same batch, so conditioning changes the batch distribution. The fixed-batch identity in Appendix A.3 does not establish Eq. (17) for the stated population objective. Moreover, interpreting the adaptive algorithm as optimizing a smoothed objective requires distinguishing frozen-basis derivatives from derivatives through A(W). This is a material gap in a central theoretical claim.

Soundness—the alignment result does not cover the implemented update: Eq. (22) uses an isolated-layer directional derivative, whereas Algorithm 2 perturbs all layers simultaneously and shares a scalar containing contributions from every layer. Those contributions affect expected layerwise cosine similarity and cannot simply be omitted. The spectral condition in Eq. (33) is also not empirically verified, and the analysis assumes exact leading singular vectors rather than the approximate bases actually used.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are insufficient. Section 6 reports validation-based grid search but omits the search ranges, selected learning rates, most perturbation settings, training batch sizes, prompting details, precise evaluation metrics and splits, and seed counts. Tables provide no uncertainty estimates, which matters particularly for small datasets such as CB and COPA. The manuscript does not provide code or enough configuration detail to reliably reproduce the comparisons.

Baseline fidelity needs clarification. Eq. (2) presents MeZO using a one-sided difference, whereas standard MeZO uses symmetric positive and negative perturbations. Whether the experiments alter that baseline is unclear. Because finite-difference bias can affect performance, superiority over the established method needs comparison against its standard implementation with documented tuning.

The mechanism is insufficiently isolated. Experiments use rank one, but Figure 1 shows weak rank-one gradient capture for several layers, and even rank ten does not uniformly approach one as the text suggests. There are no rank or power-iteration ablations, nor a matched random orthonormal-subspace control separating activation guidance from perturbation normalization. Figure 2 provides only one model/task diagnostic and omits LOZO.

Practical significance and limitations need better calibration. Evaluation is limited to 0.6B–1B models, and no wall-clock measurements substantiate the claim that subspace extraction adds little computational cost. ZO receives 20,000 steps versus 1,000 for FO; memory comparisons do not include memory-efficient FO alternatives. These limitations do not invalidate the observed gains, but the broad efficiency and superiority claims exceed the evidence. Together with the theoretical and reproducibility gaps, they prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality: Using current minibatch activations to guide ZO perturbations is a useful extension of data-independent low-rank perturbations. Although the identity G = QHᵀ is standard, its use to construct inexpensive, activation-informed search spaces provides a concrete methodological contribution.

Significance: The reported results suggest practical value for memory-constrained fine-tuning. AGZO improves over both ZO baselines on most evaluated tasks across several model sizes. Figures 3 and 4 show only approximately 0.01–0.04 GB additional peak memory relative to the ZO baselines.

Soundness: The fixed-subspace, single-layer cosine formula in Theorem 5.4 gives an informative characterization of the trade-off between captured gradient magnitude and search dimension. The rank and power-iteration ablations provide supporting evidence, including near-exact-SVD alignment with three power iterations.

Presentation: The core algorithm is understandable, with explicit pseudocode for subspace extraction, seed-based perturbation regeneration, and in-place updates. The appendix usefully reports throughput and acknowledges that larger-model and LoRA comparisons have limited scope. No material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—population smoothing claims do not cover the implemented estimator. Algorithm 2 constructs A from the same minibatch used to evaluate the loss, so A and B are dependent. Appendix A.1 establishes a valid identity for a fixed batch and fixed basis, but averaging does not generally yield Proposition 5.1's projected gradient of the unconditional population objective. In the small-step limit, the relevant expectation is E_B[∇f(W;B)P_A(W,B)], which cannot generally be factored into ∇F(W)P_A. Conditioning on A also changes the batch distribution. The dependence on W requires an explicit frozen-basis derivative convention. These distinctions materially weaken the claim that AGZO optimizes the stated subspace-smoothed objective.

Soundness—the directional superiority analysis changes the estimator. Algorithm 2 perturbs all layers simultaneously, giving the noiseless scalar sum_j ⟨G_j, Δ_j⟩. Theorem 5.4 and Appendix A.2 instead analyze a layer update with scalar ⟨G_l, Δ_l⟩. Contributions from other layers cannot simply be discarded inside the nonlinear cosine expectation. Consequently, the single-layer result does not establish the claimed layerwise or whole-model superiority of the implemented algorithm; a joint analysis is needed.

Soundness and limitations: Theorem 5.6 additionally requires exact activation rank deficiency and the upstream-gradient energy condition in Eq. (22), neither of which is validated for the main Qwen/Pangu experiments. Spectral decay alone does not ensure these conditions. Describing their failure as adversarial alignment is too strong. Moreover, Figure 1 shows very low rank-1 gradient capture in several layers, whereas all main experiments use rank 1. The rank ablation is helpful, but does not establish the theoretical assumptions or justify equating improved instantaneous cosine with better convergence.

Evaluation: The comparisons use modified baseline estimators without adequately establishing their fidelity or tuning. Eq. (2) presents MeZO using f(W+μu)−f(W), whereas standard MeZO uses symmetric finite differences. This matters because AGZO obtains its activation basis from the unperturbed evaluation. All methods also share μ despite substantially different perturbation norms, and no perturbation-scale sensitivity is reported. Appendix B uses μ=10⁻⁷ with FP32 and μ=10⁻⁴ with BF16; numerical diagnostics are needed to establish reliable loss differences and parameter restoration at these scales.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence: The manuscript omits essential settings including actual learning-rate grids and selected values, training batch sizes and sequence lengths, prompts, dataset splits/subsampling, evaluation metric definitions, seed counts, and substantial FO/LoRA configuration details. The OpenMathReasoning evaluation protocol is particularly unclear. No uncertainty estimates are reported, although several gains are small—for example, Qwen3-4B MultiRC improves from 0.852 to 0.853 over LOZO. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of robustness.

Significance and presentation: Equal iteration budgets establish query comparability, not equal computational cost. Table 7 gives 1.517 versus 2.302 steps/s for AGZO versus MeZO on COPA, yet no performance-versus-wall-clock comparison is provided. The FO comparison uses 1,000 steps versus 20,000 ZO steps, and memory results do not establish competitiveness against optimized backpropagation configurations. Claims of consistent superiority also overlook losses on BoolQ. Finally, Section 6.3 evaluates GPU-trained models on NPUs but attributes differences to optimization perturbations, while Appendix B.4 incorrectly calls Qwen3-8B an additional model family. Overall, the promising practical idea is outweighed by unresolved theoretical and experimental gaps.

strengths: Originality: Using forward-pass activations to guide ZO perturbations is a sensible, useful extension of data-independent low-rank perturbations. Although the gradient identity G = QHᵀ is standard, its application to constructing inexpensive, data-dependent ZO search spaces is a discernible contribution.

Significance: The reported downstream improvements span several tasks and model sizes. For example, on Qwen3-0.6B, AGZO improves CB from MeZO’s 0.803 to 0.892 and RTE from 0.732 to 0.772. Appendix B additionally includes 8B results, a LoRA comparison, throughput measurements, and rank and power-iteration ablations.

Soundness: The fixed-subspace Gaussian projection identity and the isolated-layer cosine formula provide useful mathematical insight within their stated idealizations. Figures 3 and 4 also support the practical claim that storing compact activation bases adds little peak memory relative to the evaluated ZO baselines.

Presentation and ethics: The algorithm is understandable, with explicit pseudocode for subspace extraction and parameter updates. The appendix acknowledges computational overhead and appropriately limits its interpretation of the LoRA comparison. No specific material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—population smoothing claim: Proposition 5.1 does not adequately account for A being constructed from the same minibatch B used to estimate the update. Appendix A.1 proves an identity with a fixed basis and then claims that averaging over B simply replaces f with F. For the implemented algorithm, the small-μ expectation instead involves E_B[∇f(W;B)P_A(W,B)], which generally cannot be replaced by a fixed projection of ∇F(W). Conditioning on A also changes the distribution of B. Moreover, interpreting Equation 11 as an objective with a W-dependent basis requires distinguishing a frozen-basis derivative from the total derivative. The per-batch identity is useful, but the claimed population-objective interpretation is not established.

Soundness—alignment theorem does not analyze the implemented layer update: Algorithm 2 perturbs all layers simultaneously and uses one shared scalar, which approaches Σ_j⟨G_j,Δ_j⟩. Theorem 5.4 instead analyzes the isolated-layer estimator ⟨G_l,Δ_l⟩Δ_l. Contributions from other layers affect the sign and cosine of the actual layer update; their cancellation in the mean-estimator calculation does not justify dropping them inside expected cosine similarity. Thus, the theorem does not establish the claimed layerwise superiority of the implemented algorithm. A full-model analysis or an explicitly restricted interpretation is needed.

Soundness and limitations: Theorem 5.6 requires exact activation rank deficiency and the upstream-energy condition in Equation 22, neither of which is established across the evaluated models. Rapid spectral decay alone does not imply that leading activation directions capture leading gradient directions. Figure 1 shows substantial layer variation at rank 1, the setting used throughout training. The appendix ablations are helpful, but a single-task rank study and GPT-2 diagnostic do not establish these assumptions broadly or provide a convergence guarantee.

Reproducibility and evidential strength: The manuscript does not report repeated-run variability, selected learning rates or search grids, main-task batch sizes and sequence lengths, prompt templates, sufficiently explicit evaluation splits and metrics, or detailed FO/LoRA configurations. These omissions are consequential when several improvements are only a few tenths of a percentage point. The OpenMathReasoning result also lacks a sufficiently specified evaluation protocol. The reported pseudocode and common codebase do not resolve these gaps.

Comparison fairness and practical significance: Equations 2 and 4 describe one-sided baseline estimators; standard MeZO uses symmetric two-point differences, so the baseline modification needs justification and comparison with the established implementation. A shared μ does not equalize perturbation magnitude across dense and orthonormal-subspace directions. Equal training steps also do not imply equal computational budgets: Table 7 reports 1.517 steps/s for AGZO versus 2.302 for MeZO on COPA. Equal-wall-clock comparisons and clearer tuning details are needed, particularly before interpreting the 20,000-step ZO versus 1,000-step FO comparison.

Presentation and claim calibration: Repeated claims of consistent superiority overlook counterexamples such as BoolQ in Tables 1 and 2. Section 6.3 evaluates GPU-trained models on NPUs but attributes differences partly to perturbations during optimization, which does not explain an inference-only platform change. Appendix B.4 incorrectly characterizes additional Qwen3 results as evidence from another model family. These issues, together with the theoretical gaps, make the central claims stronger than the supporting evidence.

strengths: Originality: Using current minibatch activations to guide zeroth-order perturbations is a useful distinction from the data-independent perturbations of MeZO and LOZO. The gradient factorization in Eq. (5) is standard, but its use to construct compact, forward-only perturbation subspaces is a meaningful methodological contribution.

Significance: Memory-constrained fine-tuning is an important application. Figures 3 and 4 support the claim that activation guidance adds negligible peak memory relative to the evaluated ZO baselines. Reported downstream improvements span several model sizes and tasks; for example, Qwen3-0.6B CB improves from 0.803 with MeZO to 0.892 with AGZO.

Soundness within the idealized setting: The fixed-subspace, single-layer cosine formula in Theorem 5.4 provides useful insight into the trade-off between gradient capture and sampling dimension. The rank and power-iteration ablations provide complementary empirical evidence, including near-exact-SVD alignment with three power iterations.

Presentation and limitations: The main algorithm is understandable, with explicit pseudocode and a clear memory argument. The appendix usefully reports throughput costs and qualifies the LoRA and larger-model comparisons. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—population smoothing claim: Proposition 5.1 does not follow for the implemented batch-dependent subspaces. Algorithm 2 constructs A from the same minibatch used to evaluate the loss. Appendix A.3 establishes a valid identity for a fixed batch and frozen basis, but averaging does not permit replacing the batch loss with F while retaining a common projector. In the zero-radius limit, the actual expectation is E_B[∇f(W;B)P_A(B)], generally not ∇F(W)P_A. Dependence of A on W also requires an explicitly frozen-basis interpretation. Consequently, the claim that the actual algorithm estimates the projected gradient of the stated population-smoothed objective needs correction.

Soundness—alignment theorem does not cover the actual layer updates: Algorithm 2 perturbs all layers simultaneously, so its noiseless scalar is the sum over layers of ⟨G_j, Δ_j⟩. Theorem 5.4 and Appendix A.2 instead use only ⟨G_l, Δ_l⟩ for a layer's estimator. Other layers' contributions cannot be discarded inside the nonlinear cosine expectation. Thus, the theorem is valid for an isolated-layer oracle but does not establish the claimed layer-wise superiority of the implemented algorithm. A full-model analysis or explicitly narrower claim is needed.

The sufficient conditions for superiority are not adequately connected to practice. Theorem 5.6 assumes exact activation rank deficiency and the upstream-energy condition in Eq. (22), whereas the experiments mainly demonstrate spectral decay. Neither effective low rank nor gradient confinement to the full activation span guarantees these conditions for the rank-one basis actually used. Figure 1 also shows substantially weaker rank-one gradient capture in several layers. Higher instantaneous cosine similarity alone does not establish better convergence.

Experimental uncertainty and reproducibility are insufficient. Tables report point estimates without seed counts or variability, although several gains are small—for example, 0.853 versus 0.852 on Qwen3-4B MultiRC. Appendix B omits selected learning rates and search grids, training batch sizes and sequence lengths, prompts, evaluation metrics and split details, LOZO configuration, and LoRA hyperparameters. The added OpenMathReasoning experiment lacks a defined evaluation protocol. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of comparative gains.

Baseline fidelity and practical efficiency need stronger evaluation. Eq. (2) presents MeZO using a forward difference rather than its usual symmetric estimator; the manuscript should clarify and justify the implementation used. Equal ZO step counts establish equal query budgets, not equal computational budgets: Table 7 reports 1.517 steps/s for AGZO versus 2.302 for MeZO on COPA. Time-to-quality comparisons and a memory-aware first-order baseline would better establish practical value, especially given the 20,000-step ZO versus 1,000-step FO comparison.

Presentation overstates the evidence in several places. Claims of consistent superiority have exceptions, including BoolQ in Tables 1 and 2. Appendix B.4 calls additional Qwen3-8B results evidence beyond Qwen3/Pangu and an additional model family, which they are not. Section 6.3 evaluates GPU-trained models on NPUs, so its explanation involving perturbations during optimization does not explain that experiment. Overall, the promising idea and memory results do not outweigh the unresolved central theoretical claims and evaluation gaps.
